*   **Logical Bank Size:** Each individual logical bank covers a volume of $16^3$ voxels [S1].
The evidence explicitly states in the notes and the main text of Source [S1] that 'the effective size of each individual bank... is 16^3' voxels. This directly matches the claim.
supported

*   **Measured Performance:** On a $256^3$ voxel dataset (CT scan of a human foot), the difference in frame rate between the four DIMMs architecture and the eight logical memories architecture is always less than 1 frame per second [S1].

The evidence explicitly states in Section 4 (Results) that 'the difference between the results for the four DIMMs and eight logical memories is always less than 1 frame per second.' Additionally, Section 5 confirms that the 'Foot' dataset is a 'CT scan of the front part of a human foot with 256^3 voxels.' Therefore, all facts in the claim are present and supported by the text.
supported
1.  **Map Subcubes to Banks:** Divide the voxel space into subcubes and place neighboring subcubes in the x, y, and z directions into neighboring SDRAM banks [S1].

The claim states that neighboring subcubes in the x, y, and z directions are placed into neighboring SDRAM banks. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in Section 3.2: 'If we take the row size of one bank of a SDRAM and place the neighbouring subcubes in the x,y and z directions into neighbouring SDRAM banks we can place three into the same SDRAM and use a second SDRAM to provide four more banks for the remaining neighbouring subcubes...'
supported
It builds on the VIZARD II design which proposed 32 bits per voxel [S1].

The source text explicitly states: 'If we want to have 32 bits per voxel as proposed in the original VIZARD II design then two 16bit wide devices will be required per logical memory.' This confirms that the VIZARD II design proposed 32 bits per voxel and that the current design (Eight Logical Memories) builds upon or implements this specification.
supported

2.  **Distribute Across SDRAMs:** Assign three of the neighboring subcubes to the same physical SDRAM device and assign the remaining four neighboring subcubes to a second physical SDRAM device, assuming 4 banks per SDRAM [S1]. (Note: The source describes a 3+4 distribution totaling seven subcubes, while naming the architecture eight logical memories [S1].)

The claim accurately reflects the details provided in Source [S1]. The source explicitly states that in the 'Eight Logical Memories' architecture, one can 'place three into the same SDRAM and use a second SDRAM to provide four more banks for the remaining neighbouring subcubes, assuming 4 banks per SDRAM.' It also mentions the context of 'eight logical memory banks' and the specific distribution of subcubes into these banks.
supported
4.  **Issue Precharge Commands:** When a ray passes into the neighborhood of the eight banks, issue a precharge command across all eight banks simultaneously [S1].

The claim states that when a ray passes into the neighborhood of the eight banks, a precharge command is issued across all eight banks simultaneously. Source [S1] explicitly states in Section 3.2: 'When a ray passes into the neighbourhood of the eight banks a precharge is issued across all eight banks so that a switch between banks will only take as much time as a bank activate instead of a precharge and activate command.' This confirms the fact in the claim.
supported

It replicates data to allow fetching eight voxels, storing two consecutive voxels instead of one [S1].

The claim states that the system replicates data to allow fetching eight voxels and stores two consecutive voxels instead of one. Source [S1] explicitly states: 'Using only four DIMM modules limits the number of individual memory addresses. Hence, fetching the eight voxels... is only feasible... by replicating data.' It further confirms: 'As a result of the data replication, we need to store two consecutive voxels instead of one.' Both parts of the claim are directly supported by the text.
supported

*   **Strengths:** Practical solution leveraging modern SDRAM switching characteristics; near-optimal performance; enables a single PCI board solution running at full 100MHz [S1].

The claim states that the evidence supports a practical solution leveraging modern SDRAM switching characteristics, offers near-optimal performance, and enables a single PCI board solution running at full 100MHz. Source [S1] explicitly mentions: 1) 'taking advantage of the shorter switching times between banks in modem SDRAMs' (modern SDRAM switching characteristics); 2) 'a near optimal and more practical solution'; and 3) 'enabling a single PC1board solution running at full 1OOMHz' (PCI board at 100MHz). All facts in the claim are present in the evidence.
